title: Different answers
hook: teshuvah, grace, mercy, karma's release, reciprocity: forgiveness means different things in each home
carry: kept whole, in its own words

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power in Ramadan's last nights. Your line was the night of power.

Five cards on a kitchen table, face up. Teshuvah. Grace. Mercy. Release. Reciprocity. Flip any one over, and the back reads the same English word: forgiveness. For weeks, this block has visited homes that each keep that word in a different room. Tomorrow the question closes. Today the cards go side by side: not to choose a winner, not to blend them into one, just to see each clearly, in its own home. Different answers to the same human need.
screen: `FIVE CARDS, ONE WORD ON THE BACK.` → `EACH IN ITS OWN HOME.`

segments.voice: First, teshuvah, a Hebrew word that means return. The Jewish teacher Maimonides lays it out as a path: leave the wrong, regret it, resolve not to go back to it, and confess it. For wrongs against people, Jewish teaching adds making it right with the person hurt. Forgiveness here is a road someone walks back along. Second, grace, a Christian word. Christian teaching speaks of forgiveness as a gift from God that no one earns, and of passing that gift on. The Lord's Prayer puts the two side by side, in the King James words: "And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors." Third, mercy. The Qur'an tells people who have wronged themselves not to despair of God's mercy, and calls God the Forgiving, the Merciful. Fourth, two more answers, from the East. The first is release. In Jain teaching, holding on to anger binds karma to the soul, and asking and giving forgiveness loosens it. The Buddhist Dhammapada points the same way: hatred never ends by hatred, only by its opposite. The second is reciprocity. Confucius is asked for one word to live by. His answer, in Legge's translation: "What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others." Some of these overlap. Some don't. Each tradition would want its answer kept whole, in its own words, not stirred into the others. The point isn't which one is right. It's that forgiveness has been thought about with great care, in many homes, and there's more than one way in.
screen: `TESHUVAH — THE ROAD BACK.` · `GRACE — A GIFT PASSED ON.` · `MERCY — DO NOT DESPAIR.` · `RELEASE AND RECIPROCITY.` · then, large: `DIFFERENT ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Read the five words to yourself, slowly: return, gift, mercy, release, reciprocity, and notice which one stays with you, without deciding why. Then write one sentence, on paper or your phone, that begins: forgiveness, to me, is. Let it be your own words, not the right words; if you pray, you can hold the sentence in your prayer.
Different answers. Return, grace, mercy, release and reciprocity: the shapes forgiveness takes in different homes, each kept whole. Today's word.
Your line: kept whole, in its own words. Five homes, five answers, none of them stirred into the others. Day nine hundred ninety-seven, done.

howItsDone: On this path, people study each tradition's teaching on forgiveness in its own words, and some keep a journal where they write what forgiveness means to them.

chat.says: Isn't forgiveness basically the same idea in every religion?
options: Some parts match, but each keeps its shape: turning back, free gift, mercy, letting go, give-and-take.
Yes, they all mean exactly the same thing, just said in different languages and words.
No, they're total opposites; each one rejects everything the others say about forgiving.
